The (Re-)Synchronising Therapy Method

STM — an integrative method grounded in the Resonance Theory of Consciousness

Therapy

Two methods: STM (this page) and its movement core MBMR, which forms the physical backbone within STM.

What the (Re-)Synchronising Therapy Method is

The (Re-)Synchronising Therapy Method, STM for short, is a form of psychological and philosophical guidance for adults who are stuck with anxiety, low mood, stress, tension, difficult experiences from the past, physical complaints without a clear medical cause, or questions about identity and meaning.

The core idea is simple. Your inner life resembles music: all kinds of processes in your body and mind play together. When they are well attuned, your experience feels whole, coherent and alive. With complaints that attunement is disturbed; you fall out of time, as it were. STM helps you restore that inner attunement, so that you feel more whole, present and resilient again. Hence the word “re-synchronising”: coming back into sync.

STM is not a separate new technique. It is a way of working that brings proven forms of therapy together (talking therapy, explanation and insight, movement and body work, mindfulness, hypnotherapy, EMDR and short-term depth psychology) and determines per person which of these, and in what order, help most.

The method is based on the Resonance Theory of Consciousness (RTC), the research on which the practitioner is writing his thesis.

STM is offered by an academically trained psychologist working independently and autonomously. Read more under About.

The idea behind it, simply put

Two ways of experiencing. You can relate to your experience in two ways. The first is direct experiencing: feeling what is here now, in your body and around you, without immediately judging it. The second is thinking about it: naming, judging, explaining, comparing, giving yourself a label. Both are needed. But with complaints, thinking often takes over. You spend a lot of time “in your head”, you ruminate, you lose contact with direct feeling.

Old contemplative traditions have words for this. Avidya means “not-seeing”: losing contact with how your experience actually is. Dukkha means “suffering” or “inner fragmentation”: what follows from it. In this method we call the personal form this takes in you the pathologos: the particular structure of your being stuck. The psychological assessment at the start maps that structure.

Rhythm and time. Your experience has a rhythm. Under stress and anxiety that rhythm speeds up; everything fragments, you feel rushed, you jump from one thing to the next, you become exhausted. In low mood it slows down instead; everything feels sluggish, flat and empty. STM helps bring your rhythm back to a more comfortable pace, mainly through movement, breath and attention.

Becoming whole again. Recovery does not mean you will never feel anything again, or that you will always be calm. It means you can move fluidly between states again, that you have a stable sense of “now” that can also carry difficult things, and that you are no longer stuck in the same groove.

Who it is for, and when it is not

Suited to

Anxiety and panic, low mood and depressive complaints, chronic stress and overstrain, the aftermath of difficult or overwhelming experiences, physical complaints in which tension plays a part, rumination and worry, feelings of estrangement or emptiness, and questions about who you are and what matters.

Not suited, or other care first

An acute crisis or strong thoughts of suicide, psychosis or untreated bipolar disorder, a severe addiction that needs attention first, or a physical condition that rules out exertion (in which case we adapt the movement component or refer you). In those cases we look together at what you need now and refer you on where appropriate. STM is not a crisis service.

What a programme looks like

1. Introduction and intake (two 60-minute sessions). In the first conversation we get acquainted and you map out your complaints, your background and what you are asking for. In the second we discuss the questionnaire results, I explain the model, and together we formulate your pathologos and your goals. After that we make practical arrangements.

2. Questionnaires. At the start you complete three scientifically grounded questionnaires: the NVM (on personality characteristics), the SCL-90 (on complaints) and the UCL (on how you handle problems). They help us clarify the nature and severity of your complaints and track your progress. We repeat the complaints list a few times during the programme and at the end. A score is a snapshot and a tool, not a stamp. Your data is treated confidentially in line with privacy legislation.

3. The treatment, in phases.

  • Phase 1: calm and solid ground. First we make sure you stand more firmly: explanation, breathing, grounding exercises, attention to sleep and lifestyle, and where needed a plan for difficult moments.
  • Phase 2: movement and presence. We work with mindful movement and walking or running with attention, with breath and with mindfulness. This brings your rhythm back and strengthens contact with your body and the present moment.
  • Phase 3: loosening what is stuck. Now we address the core: with talking therapy and short-term depth psychology we look at recurring patterns; with EMDR we process circumscribed difficult memories; with hypnotherapy and exercises we loosen stuck reactions.
  • Phase 4: anchoring. We make sure what you have achieved lasts: freer movement, meaning and values, relapse prevention, and a calm tapering off with one or two follow-up appointments.

The phases do not run strictly one after another; we step back when needed and go at your pace.

4. A 60-minute session, step by step.

± 5 min briefly arriving and looking back on the past week
± 5 min setting the focus for today together
± 5 min a short exercise with breath, attention or body awareness to settle and make contact
± 30 min the actual work with one or two suitable techniques
± 8 min pausing at what it brought you and anchoring that
± 5 min taking home an exercise or assignment
± 2 min closing with a short check

The techniques we can use

We choose together what suits you. Possible are:

  • Talking therapy. Exploratory conversations in which you come to understand yourself and your history better and start to recognise recurring patterns.
  • Explanation and insight (psycho-education). Clear explanation about your complaints and about what helps, so that you gain more grip yourself.
  • Movement and body work (MBMR). Walking or running with attention, rhythmic exercises and breath work, to restore your inner rhythm and strengthen contact with your body. This is a method of the practitioner’s own research.
  • Mindfulness. Training non-judgemental attention for the present moment; helps especially with rumination, stress and preventing relapse.
  • Hypnotherapy. Working with a calm, inwardly directed state of attention to loosen stuck reactions and strengthen your inner resources. Always with your consent and under your direction.
  • EMDR. A proven method for letting difficult memories lose their charge, in which you hold the memory while following eye movements or taps.
  • Short-term psychodynamic therapy. A focused, time-limited form of depth psychology around a core theme.

What can you expect as a result?

In the practitioner’s practice, people who completed a full programme showed broad relief of complaints: not only less of one complaint, but less anxiety, low mood, physical tension, irritability and sleep problems at the same time. That fits the idea behind the method: when the underlying coherence recovers, much improves at once.

At the same time we are honest: there are no guarantees. How much you gain also depends on your situation and on what you practise yourself between sessions. STM does not replace your GP, a psychiatrist or medication; where needed we work together with them. The integral framework of STM rests on a worked-out theory and on practice-based research, but as a whole it has not yet been tested in large comparative studies. The individual techniques we use have been.

Practical

Cost the standard rate is 100 euro per 60-minute session
Adjusted rate if you cannot afford the standard rate, there is room for an adjusted, income-dependent rate. In a short conversation we look together at your income situation and agree a lower amount on a graduated scale: the lower the income, the lower the rate. That keeps the guidance accessible on a tighter budget. You simply raise it at the introductory meeting; there is no separate application or complicated procedure.
Frequency usually weekly or fortnightly
Duration generally two intake conversations, then around twelve to twenty sessions, and one or two follow-up appointments. This differs per person.
Cancelling at least 24 hours in advance please; otherwise costs may be charged (exact terms are in the treatment agreement)
Reimbursement STM is uninsured care; health insurers generally do not reimburse this guidance. Please note that you pay for the sessions yourself.
Location at the practice in Zwaag; part of it can be online by arrangement
Applying through the registration form on this website. You fill in your name, contact details and a short description of what you are asking for. Do not put medical or sensitive details in the form; we discuss those in the first conversation. After you apply we get in touch within a few working days for an introduction.

Example of the income-dependent rate

The amounts below are indicative and serve as an example; we agree the exact rate together at the introductory meeting. You do not need to bring proof of income; we work from an honest conversation and trust.

Rate Approximate income (gross per year, household) Per session
Standard above 45,000 euro, or your employer or an agency pays 100 euro
Reduced 32,000 to 45,000 euro 75 euro
Strongly reduced 22,000 to 32,000 euro 55 euro
Minimum below 22,000 euro, benefits, or student without income 40 euro

If your income changes during the programme, we adjust the rate. If you live alone, the same amounts apply to your own income.

About the practitioner

Edward F. Hillenaar is an academically trained psychologist and philosopher. He connects scientific psychology with philosophy and contemplative traditions and, on the basis of his research — the Resonance Theory of Consciousness — developed the MBMR and STM methods. He is working towards completing his thesis.

He works independently and autonomously, with his own integrative therapy method grounded in his theory of consciousness. What that way of working involves and whether it suits you, we discuss openly at the introductory meeting, so that you can make an informed choice.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to believe in something “spiritual”? No. The method uses concepts from philosophy and from contemplative traditions, but the treatment itself consists of ordinary, recognisable psychological techniques.

Do I have to be able to run for the movement part? No. We start with walking and build up at your pace. With physical limitations we adapt it.

Is hypnotherapy safe? Will I lose control? No. You remain conscious and in charge throughout. Hypnosis is a form of concentrated attention; you do nothing you do not want to do.

Can I stop whenever I want? Yes. You set the pace yourself and can always discuss or end the programme.

Does this also work alongside medication or treatment with a psychiatrist? Yes, that can go well together. With your consent we coordinate with your GP or psychiatrist.

How does the practitioner work? As an academically trained psychologist, independently and autonomously, with his own integrative therapy method grounded in his research into consciousness. What that means precisely and whether it suits you, we discuss openly at the introductory meeting.

Important

Important

STM is not a crisis service and is not available for emergencies. In acute distress or with thoughts of suicide: call your GP or the out-of-hours GP service, call 112, or call 113 Suicide Prevention (0800-0113, free, day and night).
